headline.main: DER SPIEGEL Journalist in Gaza: Don't Allow Ghada to Die!
headline.social: DER SPIEGEL Journalist in Gaza: Don't Allow Ghada to Die!

intro: DER SPIEGEL depends on reporters in the Gaza Strip for its coverage of the war there. One of them is Ghada Alkurd. She has been working tirelessly since the beginning of the war - but now she and her family are facing starvation.
text:
Journalists must often walk a fine line: Their task is to describe, explain and analyze events without losing objectivity. They must capture and communicate emotions, pain and suffering without being overwhelmed by their own empathy as a witness. We are there to observe and inform, not to intervene. Particularly in times of crisis, this can be an immense challenge.
For the last several years, I have reported from countries stricken by war, conflict and disaster. I experienced neighbors dying in Beirut in the massive explosion that struck the port. In Afghanistan, I didn’t just report, but also sought to help save friends and colleagues from the Taliban together with other journalists. In Ukraine, I was there when our photographer received a message that Russian rockets had struck just a few meters from her parents’ home. In Israel, I didn’t just interview survivors of the October 7 attack and speak to family members of the hostages, I also sensed the deep trauma felt by Israeli friends.
But nothing could have prepared me to report on the war in the Gaza Strip. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering the Gaza Strip ever since the Hamas attack. The Israeli army has organized tours for members of the press, but journalists must adhere to a strict set of rules. And they only end up seeing what the Israeli government wants them to see. In January 2024, I took part in such a tour, and during the five hours it lasted, I didn’t see even a single Palestinian. Which means that if we want to report on what is happening inside the Gaza Strip, we must depend on local reporters we can trust. People like the two Palestinian journalists Ghada Alkurd and Malak Tantesh. They are our local eyes and ears in this war.
We work particularly closely with Ghada, 39. When we spoke for the first time in April 2024, she was in Rafah, in the far south of the Gaza Strip. By then, Ghada had already been displaced three times. Her father, she told me, had died of the consequences of diabetes and hunger, while one of her brothers had been killed in an airstrike. Ghada’s daughters Mira and Fatima, aged 12 and 10, were in Gaza City with their father, from whom Ghada has been separated for years. She was afraid that she might also lose her daughters, from whom she was now cut off, to hunger or bombs.
Even as she lived with these personal worries, Ghada reported for us on the suffering of those around her: about a 17-year-old, who had been badly tortured in an Israeli prison; about a mother whose sick child died of malnutrition; about the destruction of the healthcare system; and about the desperate demonstrations against Hamas. There was a flicker of hope at the beginning of this year: During the ceasefire, our colleague Ghada was able to return to the northern Gaza Strip and embrace her daughters again after 16 months of separation. Sufficient food and aid supplies were finally entering the strip again.
But ever since Isreal broke the ceasefire on March 18 and implemented a complete blockade for more than two months, only slightly easing it recently, the situation in Gaza has drastically deteriorated. Israeli bombs and missiles are killing dozens of people each day, with around 1,000 people thus far losing their lives on the desperate search for food while the old system of distributing aid is largely prevented from operating. A constant stream of evacuation orders has packed residents into overcrowded areas with horrific hygienic conditions. But those are also being bombed. Only by chance was Ghada spared by a strike at a popular café on the Gaza City beach.
My colleagues and I often chat with her several times a day over WhatsApp. Even as Ghada had to mourn the deaths of yet more friends, even as she suffered from stomach pains and toothaches, she almost never complained and did what we asked of her. We, the ones who live in safety, begin our days wondering whether Ghada has survived yet another night. We are afraid that she, too, could die in an Israeli attack. And that our WhatsApp messages might go unanswered.
But we hadn’t expected that hunger would also present a risk to her life. There has been a lack of sufficient food supplies in Gaza for several months, and prices in shops and at markets have skyrocketed. But last Friday, Ghada said for the first time that she wouldn’t be able to deliver a scheduled interview on time. She was so weak and exhausted from hunger, she said, that she couldn’t think clearly – and was suffering from "terrible headaches.” She apologized.
Over the weekend, her condition grew worse. When we spoke over the phone on Monday, she spoke slowly with an audibly heavy tongue. She said that she had only been able to eat a few spoonfuls of beans and a small piece of bread. From the little that she and her brother still had, she said, they were giving almost all of it to the children. She is unable to access the money in her account because of the extremely high commissions being demanded by the payout offices and the lack of security all around.
She said she is afraid of the other starving people on the streets: "People here are turning into beasts.” She knows, Ghada wrote me, that she is strong, but she said she is unable to fight off this creeping death. She said that she spends her days crying – and drinking lots of water so that there is at least something in her stomach.
At the beginning of the week, the French news agency AFP wrote of their own Palestinian colleagues in Gaza who are also unable to work any longer because of hunger: "We refuse to watch them die." The same is true for our colleague Ghada.
